proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt joint:tests}: Calculate joint significance tests of all requested pre-treatment relative time period-specific effects. At least two pre-treatment horizons must fall in the estimation window, or three under {it:esfixedbaseperiod} with {it:timetrends} and the default {it:esrelativeto(-1)}. With fewer, no test is produced. With analytic standard errors clustered at the level of {it:i} or above, the test's p-value is severely oversized, and {it:wooldid} prints the test with a caution that its p-value is not calibrated (see {help wooldid##standarderrors:Standard Errors}). The remedies are {it:bootstrap()}, {it:permute()}, or a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells that leaves many clusters inside each cell. Under a continuous treatment the tests also require many observations per cohort-by-period cell. Refused with {it:impvalues}, and with {it:fastnose} except on the fast path {it:permute()} takes by default. Under {it:bootstrap()} and {it:permute()} the reported joint test is a bootstrap or permutation test. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt adv:ersarial}: Tests the joint hypothesis that all estimated relative time period-specific effects fall on a single line through the reference period, with the slope that fits them best. This null is adversarial toward finding pre-trend violations. The p-value comes from a minimum-distance test on the event-study coefficients and their covariance matrix. Requires {it:esfixedbaseperiod}. The default pooled reference period has no single omitted period, so there the test fails with a caution and nothing is returned. Under {it:timetrends} two periods are normalized to zero and the null reduces to every coefficient being zero. Beside each p-value, {it:wooldid} returns the unweighted OLS line through the coefficients, with 0 at the reference period. The test is cancelled with a caution when the window holds fewer than one pre-treatment and one post-treatment horizon, or fewer than three coefficients in all under {it:timetrends}, when the sample fails to realize those horizons, or when the event-study covariance is degenerate. Under {it:subgroups()} the {it:att} and {it:att_it} tests are skipped for any subgroup that lost a relative period as inestimable. A rank-deficient but not degenerate covariance gives a test at reduced rank, and without {it:bootstrap()} or {it:permute()} a caution gives the rank and degrees of freedom used, which are stored in {it:e(adversarial_df_att)} and its twins. Like {it:jointtests}, the test is severely oversized unless many clusters span each treated cohort-by-period cell, which clustering on {it:i} never gives. There, use {it:permute()}, or {it:bootstrap()} with {it:boottstat}. Without {it:boottstat} the test is absent under {it:bootstrap()}. Refused with {it:impvalues}, and with {it:fastnose} except under {it:permute()}. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt pretrendpow:er(numlist)}: Reports Roth (2022) pre-trend power diagnostics for each requested power level, in percent as integers strictly between 5 and 100, as in {it:pretrendpower(50 80)}. The diagnostics are a GLS estimate of the linear pre-trend slope with its standard error and confidence interval, the smallest linear pre-trend each pre-test would detect with that power, and the bias such a trend would imply for the pooled estimand if it continued after onset. {it:mdt_wald} is for the joint pre-trend test and {it:mdt_nis} for the test that any pre-period coefficient is individually significant under the normal reference, both at the 5% level. Requires {it:esfixedbaseperiod} and at least one pre-treatment event-study coefficient. Refused with {it:impvalues}, {it:fastnose} and {it:permute()}. Under {it:bootstrap()} the diagnostics use the bootstrap covariance. With {it:subgroups()} only the overall event studies are analysed. When only {it:att_i} or {it:att_itime} is requested the reported block is the {it:att_it} event study. The diagnostics are skipped with a caution when the pre-period covariance block is unavailable, as under {it:timetrends}, or ill-conditioned. A block of partial rank gives diagnostics at reduced rank under a caution, usually from a singleton-cell design (see condition Two under {it:e(V_es_type)} in {help wooldid##output:Working with Output}). The {it:mdt_nis} column is computed for up to 4 pre-periods. For larger designs, pass {it:e(b_es_type)}, {it:e(V_es_type)} and {it:e(numpre_type)} to Roth's {help pretrends} package. Results are returned in {it:e(roth_power_type)} and companion scalars. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt antic:ipation(integer)}: Treats the effective treatment onset as {it:ttre} minus #, so periods of anticipatory response count as treated rather than as clean pre-treatment periods. proposals.new_smcl: {pstd}{ul: Two Approaches to Estimation, Pooled versus Fixed Reference Period:} By default, {it:wooldid} compares each cohort's treated periods to a pooled reference period holding all of that cohort's pre-treatment observations. Event study estimates on this default are normalized to 0 in the earliest period reported, the pooled reference period. Under {it:esfixedbaseperiod}, every estimate compares treated cohorts' post-treatment outcomes to their outcome in one pre-treatment reference period, relative period -1 unless {it:esrelativeto()} sets another. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} The choice also changes the comparison group. Under the pooled reference period every untreated observation serves as a control: never-treated cohorts, cohorts treated after the end of the sample, and the pre-treatment periods of cohorts not yet treated, apart from any pre-treatment horizons the run asks for. Parallel trends and no anticipation must then hold across all of those periods. Under {it:esfixedbaseperiod} each treated cohort's pre-treatment periods other than the reference period carry their own indicators, and the reference period only anchors the cohort's own level. With {it:timetrends}, the period just before the reference period carries no indicator either, and the two anchor the cohort's level and trend. The period effects then come from never-treated cohorts and cohorts treated after the end of the sample alone. Cohorts not yet treated do not serve as controls. Parallel trends is needed only between each treated cohort and those cohorts, from the reference period on. This is the never-treated comparison of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021). The pooled default matches the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2023) under the conditions given in {help wooldid##comparison:Comparison with Related Estimators}. {p_end}
proposals.reason: A recent correction: kept whole, two sentences joined and a few words tightened.

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} A fixed reference period is transparent: every cohort is compared to the same relative period. A pooled one can be more precise, since it averages over more periods, but different cohorts' reference periods then hold different numbers of periods. A pooled period is a poor choice when treated cohorts' outcomes evolve differently from the comparison cohorts' before treatment. Trends shared by all cohorts are absorbed by the time fixed effects. It is also a poor choice when requesting more pre-treatment horizons than every cohort can supply. A cohort with fewer observed pre-treatment periods then takes its earliest observed period as its reference period, even where other cohorts report an effect for that period. With differing outcome trends, the event study can then show counterintuitive time paths that hide even severe parallel trends violations. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd}{ul: Invalid Estimands:} For relative-period estimates the estimand types {it:att_i}, {it:att_itime} and {it:att_it} coincide. Each weights every cohort's contribution to a relative period equally, and they differ only in cells outside that period. Event studies therefore report only {it:att} and {it:att_it}, and a request for {it:att_i} or {it:att_itime} shows the {it:att_it} results. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt sub:groups()}: Specifies the subgroup (SG) variable, whose levels define the subgroups for which {it:wooldid} computes separate estimates. The SG variable must hold non-negative integers or missing values on the observations of treated units, and its levels must be collections of cohorts i. Observations with missing values belong to no subgroup and are ignored in subgroup computations. A unit is left out only if it is missing on all of its rows. A treated unit split across subgroups, or labelled on some rows and missing on others, is refused. With {it:safety(off)}, except under {it:permute()}, such a unit enters each of its subgroups weighted by its labelled share of sample weight there, so {it:att_i} and {it:att_itime} no longer weight units equally. A partly labelled unit also draws a caution. Subgroup values are embedded in the names of stored results and plots, so values 8 or more digits long can exceed Stata's limits on names. Recode ID-style codes to small integers first, for example with {it:egen newsg = group(oldsg)}. With {it:esprelength()} greater than 0, an {it:espostlength()} of 0 is raised to 1 under a caution (see {it:espostlength()}). Not compatible with {it:impvalues}. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} {ul: Description of Approach to Subgroup Effect Estimation:} {it:wooldid} estimates treatment effects for each level of the SG variable by running the margins step within that subgroup. The regression itself is unchanged. It also reports every pairwise difference between the subgroups' overall and pre-treatment effects, each with a p-value, and a joint test that all SGs share the effect of the lowest-numbered SG. Clustered standard errors for a subgroup estimate can fail when the subgroup holds few clusters, or only one. With clustering at the level of {it:i} or above, the analytic standard error of a pairwise contrast can be degenerate. {it:wooldid} then reports that contrast, and the across-subgroup equality test covering it, without inference, under a caution naming the count. With {it:safety(off)} they are reported as computed. Under {it:permute()} the contrasts are permuted as coefficient differences and stand, and the caution counts the rows whose {it:se_analytic} is degenerate. Under {it:boottstat} each contrast is studentized by that standard error, and a caution says so when it is degenerate. The remedies are {it:permute()}, {it:bootstrap()} without {it:boottstat}, or a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} A subgroup variable that varies within a cohort-by-period cell, or over time within a unit, is refused with an informative error. Where it varies within a cell and {it:safety(off)} lets the run proceed, every subgroup estimate only reweights the same pooled cell effects. Contrasts then cannot show within-cell differences, and can come back identical when the true effects differ. The usual remedy is to define {it:i} at the finer level over which the subgroup varies, for example {it:egen newi = group(i sg), missing}. Without {it:missing}, rows with a missing subgroup value would be dropped from the estimation sample. Splitting {it:i} this way makes {it:att_i} and {it:att_itime} average over the split pseudo-units rather than over the original units. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} A triple difference is a special case. Its target is the difference between the diff-in-diff estimates of two groups, each present among both treated and control cohorts. Define {it:i} as the treatment onset cohort by group, for example {it:egen newi = group(ttre sgvarname), missing}. Specify the group variable as the SG variable and add SG by period fixed effects, as in {it:subgroups(sgvarname) fe(i.sgvarname##i.t)}. The contrast removes shocks that hit both groups in a treated cohort and period only when the two SG estimates weight the same onset-cohort-by-period cells in the same way. Use {it:att_it}, with both groups present in every treated onset-cohort-by-period cell. Its contrast is then the simple average of the cell-level triple differences. Under {it:att} each group weights its cells by the sample weight of its own observations, so that contrast keeps those shocks whenever the group shares of that weight differ across cells. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {phang}{opt contreat(varname)}: The continuous treatment variable. It must be defined for all observations, set to 0 where it has no natural value in untreated cohort-periods. Observations on which it is missing are dropped from the estimation sample. If no treated cohort-period cell has dose variation that identifies its dose slope, for example with a dose constant within each cohort, the within-cell average marginal effects are not identified. Under default safety {it:wooldid} says so, reports the ame results as missing and continues with the att results. Under {it:contreatcontrols(untreatedZero)} that design is refused instead. If only some treated cells lack within-cell dose variation, their dose slopes are not identified either and would enter the ame as zeros. {it:wooldid} drops those cells from the estimation sample with a caution, so the att and the ame are estimated on the remaining cells. The cells checked are those that carry a dose slope, which include the pre-treatment periods under {it:esfixedbaseperiod}. The number dropped is stored in {it:e(contreat_ndropcells)}, and their observations are counted in {it:e(N_dropped)}. {it:safety(off)} silences the caution but keeps the drop. A cell whose dose is zero throughout is never dropped. No cell is dropped when no cell on its side of treatment onset has dose variation. Under {it:contreatcontrols(untreatedZero)} the check does not run. Not available with {it:gteffects}. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} A lattice lets the dose slope vary within i-t cells, and it also adds treatment effect intercepts within cells, much as a finer {it:i} would. Average marginal effects do not capture those intercept jumps, nor the cell intercepts themselves. With many lattice groups the intercepts can absorb nearly all of the dose effect and threaten identification of the ame. The ame and the att can also disagree, even in sign. In such cases use a coarser lattice or rely on the att, which does capture the intercepts, above all in the continuous treatment effects plots. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} Do not over-saturate the specification with lattice terms. Each treated cohort-period cell must hold at least two distinct values of Contreat_jt within each lattice bin it occupies. That variation is all that identifies the piece's slope. Without it, one slope term in that cell drops for collinearity and the piece takes the slope of another bin in the same cell. The reported average marginal effect and the plotted average marginal effects by bin include that borrowed slope. A caution gives the number of such pieces, and {it:verbose} lists the dropped terms. Separately, a piece with no more observations than parameters is fitted exactly, and the analytic standard errors can then be far smaller than the estimates' sampling variability. As a rule of thumb, the units contributing to a treated cell should number several times the lattice bins. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} To identify the average marginal effects from dose variation within treated cohorts, without a strictly untreated control group, specify {it:contreatwithin}. {it:wooldid} still reports att estimates, but read them with care. In a period where some unit is not yet treated, a treated cell's att includes the level effect of treatment, measured against that period's untreated units. In a period with no untreated reference rows, the treated cells' level effects are not identified. {it:wooldid} then sets one cell's level effect in that period to zero, measures the other cells against it, and names those periods in a caution. The att there depends on which cell was set to zero. It can change when the cohorts are relabelled, and it can take the wrong sign. Rows moved into an {it:esprelength()} window also leave the reference pool, so the pretreatment att can be affected the same way. The att and its event study can therefore shift sharply at the last treatment onset for this reason alone. The att is the integral of the estimated average marginal effects across the dose distribution only when {it:fe()} absorbs every cohort-period level effect, for example with i-t fixed effects. Even then, it extrapolates the estimated slope down to a dose of zero. Rely on the ame results under {it:contreatwithin}. The control type {it:byTime} is refused here, since without an untreated group the time period interactions would partial out genuine treatment effects for some group. {it:safety(off)} downgrades the refusal to a caution. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} {ul:What the ame Measures:} Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. The choice of g() sets the parallel trends assumption: without treatment, units at different doses would have followed the same outcome path, apart from the dose effects g() allows for. That identifies the att, and the att within each bin of the continuous treatment effects plots. The ame is the effect of a marginal increase in the dose only under a stronger condition: units at different doses would also have gained the same from treatment at any given dose. This is the strong parallel trends assumption of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024). Without it, the ame also carries selection bias, since the units that took higher doses may simply be those that gain more from treatment. The same holds for the ame within each bin and for differences in att across bins. Where the att under {it:contreatwithin} is the integral of the ame, it needs the same stronger condition. {p_end}

proposals.new_smcl: {pstd} {ul:Continuous Treatments and Cluster-Robust Standard Errors:} With {it:cluster()} at the level of {it:i} or coarser, the analytic standard errors of the ame-family quantities are not identified. {it:wooldid} prints a caution, reports those standard errors, the ame joint tests and the ame adversarial p-values as missing, withholds {it:e(V_es_ame*)}, and draws the ame continuous treatment effects plots without confidence intervals. The att rows are still reported, but their analytic standard errors are understated in this design as well (see {help wooldid##standarderrors:What Level to Cluster At}). A cell holding a single observation does not trigger this. Valid ame inference then comes from {it:bootstrap()}, {it:permute()}, {it:impvalues}, {it:robust} when errors are independent across observations, or a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells. {p_end}
